It is more emphatical than <foreign xml:lang="el">αὐτόπται</foreign>, “eye-witnesses.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen137778" type="x-p"/> </note> We hence conclude, that they by no means serve Christ, nor are like the apostles, who presumptuously mount the pulpit to prattle of speculations unknown to themselves; for he alone is the lawful minister of Christ, who knows the truth of the doctrine which he delivers: not that all obtain certainty in the same way; for what Peter says is that he himself was present, when Christ was declared by a voice from heaven to be the Son of God. Three only were then present, but they were sufficient as witnesses; for they had through many miracles seen the glory of Christ, and had a remarkable evidence of his divinity in his resurrection. But we now obtain certainty in another way; for though Christ has not risen before our eyes, yet we know by whom his resurrection has been handed down to us. And added to this is the inward testimony of conscience, the sealing of the Spirit, which far exceeds all the evidence of the senses. But let us remember that the gospel was not at the beginning made up of vague rumors, but that the apostles were the authentic preachers of what they had seen.<div eID="gen137777" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Pet.1.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137771" osisID="2Pet.1.16" type="section"/>
entries.68c5bdf9389c45f05ac715dd49f675c44ee226ae: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Pet.1.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Pet.1.17" sID="gen137779" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">For he received from God the Father.</hi> He chose one memorable example out of many, even that of Christ, when, adorned with celestial glory, he conspicuously displayed his divine majesty to his three disciples. And though Peter does not relate all the circumstances, yet he sufficiently designates them when he says, <hi type="italic">that a voice came from the magnificent glory.</hi> For the meaning is, that nothing earthly was seen there, but that a celestial majesty shone on every side. We may hence conclude what those displays of greatness were which the evangelists relate. And it was necessarily thus done, in order that the authority of that voice which came might be more awful and solemn, as we see that it was done all at once by the Lord. For when he spoke to the fathers, he did not only cause his words to sound in the air, but by adding some symbols or tokens of his presence, he proved the oracles to be his.<div eID="gen137780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137781" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son.</hi> Peter then mentions this voice, as though it was sufficient alone, as a full evidence for the gospel, and justly so. For when Christ is acknowledged by us to be him whom the Father has sent, this is our highest wisdom. There are two parts to this sentence. When he says, “This is,” the expression is very emphatical, intimating, that he was the Messiah who had been so often promised. Whatever, then, is found in the Law and the Prophets respecting the Messiah, is declared here, by the Father, to belong to him whom he so highly commended. In the other part of the sentence, he announces Christ as his own Son, in whom his whole love dwells and centres. It hence follows that we are not otherwise loved than in him, nor ought the love of God to be sought anywhere else. It is sufficient for me now only to touch on these things by the way.<div eID="gen137781" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Pet.1.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137779" osisID="2Pet.1.17" type="section"/>
entries.d5a8287a1f224361e13c0e05131dc186a3b9d308:
18. In the holy mount. He calls it the holy mount, for the same reason that the ground was called holy where God appeared to Moses. For wherever the Lord comes, as he is the fountain of all holiness, he makes holy all things by the odor of his presence. And by this mode of speaking we are taught, not only to receive God reverently wherever he shews himself, but also to prepare ourselves for holiness, as soon as he comes nigh us, as it was commanded the people when the law was proclaimed on Mount Sinai. And it is a general truth,
“Be ye holy, for I am holy, who dwell in the midst of you.” (Leviticus 11:44; 19:2.)
2 Peter 1:19-21
19. We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
19. Et habemus firmiorem propheticum sermonem, cui bene facitis attendentes, tanquam lucernae apparenti in caliginoso loco, donee illuceat dies, et lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris;
20. Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
20. Hoc primùm cognito, quòd omnis prophetia scripturae privatae (vel, proprii motus) interpretationis non est:
21. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
21. Neque enim voluntate hominis allata est quondam prophetia; sed à Spiritu Sancto impulsi, loquuti sunt sancti Dei homines.
entries.a45102408e8b60cc290fac5e6c784145c048e637: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Pet.1.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Pet.1.19" sID="gen137794" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">We have also. </hi>He now shews that the truth of the gospel is founded on the oracles of the prophets, lest they who embraced it should hesitate to devote themselves wholly to Christ: for they who waver cannot be otherwise than remiss in their minds. But when he says, “We have,” he refers to himself and other teachers, as well as to their disciples. The apostles had the prophets as the patrons of their doctrine; the faithful also sought from them a confirmation of the gospel. I am the more disposed to take this view, because he speaks of the whole Church, and makes himself one among others. At the same time, he refers more especially to the Jews, who were well acquainted with the doctrine of the prophets. And hence, as I think, he calls their word <hi type="italic">more sure</hi> or <hi type="italic">firmer</hi><div eID="gen137795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137796" type="x-p"/>For they who take the comparative for a positive, that is, “more sure,” for “sure,” do not sufficiently consider the whole context. The sense also is a forced one, when it is said to be “more sure,” because God really completed what he had promised concerning his Son. For the truth of the gospel is here simply proved by a twofold testimony, — that Christ had been highly approved by the solemn declaration of God, and, then, that all the prophecies of the prophets confirmed the same thing. But it appears at first sight strange, that the word of the prophets should be said to be more sure or firmer than the voice which came from the holy mouth of God himself; for, first, the authority of God's word is the same from the beginning; and, secondly, it was more confirmed than previously by the coming of Christ. But the solution of this knot is not difficult: for here the Apostle had a regard to his own nation, who were acquainted with the prophets, and their doctrine was received without any dispute. As, then, it was not doubted by the Jews but that all the things which the prophets had taught, came from the Lord, it is no wonder that Peter said that their word was more sure. Antiquity also gains some reverence. There are, besides, some other circumstances which ought to be noticed; particularly, that no suspicion could be entertained as to those prophecies in which the kingdom of Christ had so long before been predicted.<div eID="gen137796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137797" type="x-p"/>The question, then, is not here, whether the prophets deserve more credit than the gospel; but Peter regarded only this, to shew how much deference the Jews paid to those who counted the prophets as God's faithful ministers, and had been brought up from childhood in their school. <note n="159"> <div sID="gen137798" type="x-p"/> Much has been written on this subject; and the difficulty has arisen from a wrong construction of the passage, which is literally as follows: — “And we have more firm the prophetic word,” <foreign xml:lang="el">Καὶ ἔχομεν βεβαιότερον τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον</foreign>, that is, we have rendered more firm the prophetic word. This is confirmed by what follows; for the prophetic word is compared to “a light shining in a dark place,” and, therefore, not clear nor firm until it be fulfilled; but they were doing well to attend to this light until the full light of the gospel shone in their hearts. As<hi type="italic"> Scott</hi> maintains, the reference here is clearly to the experience of Christians to their real knowledge of divine truths; for it was to be <hi type="italic">in</hi> their <hi type="italic">hearts</hi>, and not <hi type="italic">before</hi> their <hi type="italic">eyes</hi><div eID="gen137798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137799" type="x-p"/>A great deal of learning has been spent to no purpose on this passage. It has been by most taken as granted, that “the power and coming of our Lord,” mentioned in verse 16th, is his second coming, when the whole passage refers only and expressly to his first coming. And on this gratuitous and even false supposition is grounded the elaborate exposition of <hi type="italic">Sherlock, Horsley</hi>, and others. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen137799" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen137797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137800" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Whereunto ye do well.</hi> This passage is, indeed, attended with some more difficulty; for it may be asked, what is the day which Peter mentions? To some it seems to be the clear knowledge of Christ, when men fully acquiesce in the gospel; and the <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> they explain as existing, when they, as yet, hesitate in suspense, and the doctrine of the gospel is not received as indubitable; as though Peter praised those Jews who were searching for Christ in the Law and the Prophets, and were advancing, as by this preceding light towards Christ, the Sun of righteousness, as they were praised by Luke, who, having heard Paul preaching, searched the Scripture to know whether what he said was true. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.11">Acts 17:11</reference>)<div eID="gen137800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137801" type="x-p"/>But in this view there is, first, an inconsistency, because it thus seems that the use of the prophecies is confined to a short time, as though they would be superfluous when the gospel-light is seen. Were one to object and say, that this does not necessarily follow, because <hi type="italic">until</hi> does not always denote the end. To this I say, that in commands it cannot be otherwise taken: “Walk until you finish your course;” “Fight until you conquer.” In such expressions we doubtless see that a certain time is specified. <note n="160"> <div sID="gen137802" type="x-p"/> There is no command here: the Apostle only approves of what they were doing, “whereunto ye do well that ye take heed.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen137802" type="x-p"/> </note> But were I to concede this point, that the reading of the prophets is not thus wholly cast aside; yet every one must see how frigid is this commendation, that the prophets are useful until Christ is revealed to us; for their teaching is necessary to us until the end of life. Secondly, we must bear in mind who they were whom Peter addressed; for he was not instructing the ignorant and novices, who were as yet in the first rudiments; but even those respecting whom he had before testified, that they had obtained the same precious faith, and were confirmed in the present truth. Surely the gross darkness of ignorance could not have been ascribed to such people. I know what some allege, that all had not made the same progress, and that here beginners who were as yet seeking Christ, are admonished.<div eID="gen137801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137803" type="x-p"/>But as it is evident from the context, that the words were addressed to the same persons, the passage must necessarily be applied to the faithful who had already known Christ, and had become partakers of the true light. I therefore extend this darkness, mentioned by Peter, to the whole course of life, and <hi type="italic">the day,</hi> I consider will then <hi type="italic">shine</hi> on us when we shall see face to face, what we now see through a glass darkly. Christ, the Sun of righteousness, indeed, shines forth in the gospel; but the darkness of death will always, in part, possess our minds, until we shall be brought out of the prison of the flesh, and be translated into heaven. This, then, will be the brightness of day, when no clouds or mists of ignorance shall intercept the bright shining of the Sun.<div eID="gen137803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137804" type="x-p"/>And doubtless we are so far from a perfect day, as our faith is from perfection. It is, therefore, no wonder that the state of the present life is called darkness, since we are far distant from that knowledge to which the gospel invites us. <note n="161"> <div sID="gen137805" type="x-p"/> The Apostle does not speak of the perfect day, but of the dawn of it, and the daystar is that which ushers in the perfect day. The gospel is the dawn and the daystar, compared with the glimmering light of prophecy, and compared too with the perfect day of the heavenly kingdom. Prophecy is useful still; for its fulfillment, found in the gospel, greatly strengthens faith. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen137805" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen137804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137806" type="x-p"/>In short, Peter reminds us that as long as we sojourn in this world, we have need of the doctrine of the prophets as a guiding light; which being extinguished, we can do nothing else but wander in darkness; for he does not disjoin the prophecies from the gospel, when he teaches us that they shine to shew us the way. His object only was to teach us that the whole course of our life ought to be guided by God's word; for otherwise we must be involved on every side in the darkness of ignorance; and the Lord does not shine on us, except when we take his word as our light.<div eID="gen137806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137807" type="x-p"/>But he does not use the comparison, <hi type="italic">light,</hi> or lamp, to intimate that the light is small and sparing, but to make these two things to correspond,--that we are without light, and can no more keep on the right way than those who go astray in a dark night; and that the Lord brings a remedy for this evil, when he lights a torch to guide us in the midst of darkness.<div eID="gen137807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137808" type="x-p"/>What he immediately adds respecting<hi type="italic"> the day star</hi> does not however seem altogether suitable to this explanation; for the real knowledge, to which we are advancing through life, cannot be called the beginning of the day. To this I reply, that different parts of the day are compared together, but the whole day in all its parts is set in opposition to that darkness, which would wholly overspread all our faculties, were not the Lord to come to our help by the light of his word.<div eID="gen137808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137809" type="x-p"/>This is a remarkable passage: we learn from it how God guides us. The Papists have ever and anon in their mouth, that the Church cannot err. Though the word is neglected, they yet imagine that it is guided by the Spirit. But Peter, on the contrary, intimates that all are immersed in darkness who do not attend to the light of the word. Therefore, except thou art resolved wilfully to cast thyself into a labyrinth, especially beware of departing even in the least thing from the rule and direction of the word. Nay, the Church cannot follow God as its guide, except it observes what the word prescribes.<div eID="gen137809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137810" type="x-p"/>In this passage Peter also condemns all the wisdom of men, in order that we may learn humbly to seek, otherwise than by our own understanding, the true way of knowledge; for without the word nothing is left for men but darkness.<div eID="gen137810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137811" type="x-p"/>It further deserves to be noticed, that he pronounces on the clearness of Scripture; for what is said would be a false eulogy, were not the Scripture fit and suitable to shew to us with certainty the right way. Whosoever, then, will open his eyes through the obedience of faith, shall by experience know that the Scripture has not been in vain called a light. It is, indeed, obscure to the unbelieving; but they who are given up to destruction are wilfully blind. Execrable, therefore, is the blasphemy of the Papists, who pretend that the light of Scripture does nothing but dazzle the eyes, in order to keep the simple from reading it. But it is no wonder that proud men, inflated with the wind of false confidence, do not see that light with which the Lord favors only little children and the humble. With a similar eulogy David commends the law of God in <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14 Bible:Ps.119.1-Ps.119.176">Psalms 19 and 119</reference>.<div eID="gen137811" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Pet.1.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137794" osisID="2Pet.1.19" type="section"/>
entries.d1cdf7619e8ad013881c194f579f05e5e562ec2e: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Pet.1.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Pet.1.20" sID="gen137812" type="section"/> <div sID="gen137813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">Knowing this first.</hi> Here Peter begins to shew how our minds are to be prepared, if we really wish to make progress in scriptural knowledge. There may at the same time be two interpretations given, if you read <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπηλύσεως</foreign> as some do, which means <hi type="italic">occurrence</hi>, <hi type="italic">impulse</hi>; or, as I have rendered it, <hi type="italic">interpretation</hi>, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐπιλύσεως</foreign>. But almost all give this meaning, that we ought not to rush on headlong and rashly when we read Scripture, confiding in our own understanding. They think that a confirmation of this follows, because the Spirit, who spoke by the prophets, is the only true interpreter of himself.<div eID="gen137813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137814" type="x-p"/>This explanation contains a true, godly, and useful doctrine, that then only are the prophecies read profitably, when we renounce the mind and feelings of the flesh, and submit to the teaching of the Spirit, but that it is an impious profanation of it; when we arrogantly rely on our own acumen, deeming that sufficient to enable us to understand it, though the mysteries contain things hidden to our flesh, and sublime treasures of life far surpassing our capacities. And this is what we have said, that the light which shines in it, comes to the humble alone.<div eID="gen137814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137815" type="x-p"/>But the Papists are doubly foolish, when they conclude from this passage, that no interpretation of a private man ought to be deemed authoritative. For they pervert what Peter says, that they may claim for their own councils the chief right of interpreting Scripture; but in this they act indeed childishly; for Peter calls interpretation <hi type="italic">private,</hi> not that of every individual, in order to prohibit each one to interpret; but he shews that whatever men bring of their own is profane. Were, then, the whole world unanimous, and were the minds of all men united together, still what would proceed from them, would be private or their own; for the word is here set in opposition to divine revelation; so that the faithful, inwardly illuminated by the Holy Spirit, acknowledge nothing but what God says in his word.<div eID="gen137815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137816" type="x-p"/>However, another sense seems to me more simple, that Peter says that Scripture came not from man, or through the suggestions of man. For thou wilt never come well prepared to read it, except thou bringest reverence, obedience, and docility; but a just reverence then only exists when we are convinced that God speaks to us, and not mortal men. Then Peter especially bids us to believe the prophecies as the indubitable oracles of God, because they have not emanated from men's own private suggestions. <note n="162"> <div sID="gen137817" type="x-p"/> There are in the main three renderings of this passage: — l. “No Prophecy of Scripture is of a private impulse,” or invention; — 2. “No prophecy of Scripture is of self-interpretation,” that is, is its own interpreter; — 3. No prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation, that is, is not to be interpreted according to the fancies of men, but according to the word of God and the guidance of his Spirit. Now which of these corresponds with the context? Clearly the first, the two others have nothing in the passage to countenance them. The next verse is evidently explanatory of this sentence, which seems at once to determine its meaning; and, as it is often the case in Scripture, the explanation is given negatively and positively. Prophecy <hi type="italic">did not</hi> come from the will of man; it <hi type="italic">did</hi> come from the Spirit of God. Besides, the importance attached to the announcement, “knowing this especially,” is not so clearly borne out as by the first exposition, because the fact that prophecy did not come from man, is everything in the question, while the other expositions contain only things of subordinate importance. Thus what goes before and comes after tends to confirm the same view.<div eID="gen137817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137818" type="x-p"/>Whether we take the conjectural reading (which only differs from the other in one small letter) or that which is found in all the MSS., it may admit of the meaning that has been given. There is either an <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐκ</foreign>, “from,” understood, or the word <hi type="italic">prophecy</hi> is to be repeated: “No prophecy of Scripture is <hi type="italic">from</hi> one's own explanation;” or, “No prophecy of Scripture is a <hi type="italic">prophecy</hi> of one's own explanation,” or interpretation, that is, as to things to come.<div eID="gen137818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137819" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Calvin</hi> has been followed in his view of this passage, among others, by <hi type="italic">Grotius, Doddridge</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Macknight</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen137819" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen137816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen137820" type="x-p"/>To the same purpose is what immediately follows, —<div eID="gen137820" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Pet.1.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen137812" osisID="2Pet.1.20" type="section"/>

But holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. They did not of themselves, or according to their own will, foolishly deliver their own inventions. The meaning is, that the beginning of right knowledge is to give that credit to the holy prophets which is due to God. He calls them the holy men of God, because they faithfully executed the office committed to them, having sustained the person of God in their ministrations. He says that they were — not that they were bereaved of mind, (as the Gentiles imagined their prophets to have been,) but because they dared not to announce anything of their own, and obediently followed the Spirit as their guide, who ruled in their mouth as in his own sanctuary. Understand by prophecy of Scripture that which is contained in the holy Scriptures.
CHAPTER 2
2 Peter 2:1-3
1. But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
1. Fuerunt autem et falsi prophetae in populo, sicuti et inter vos erunt falsi doctores, qui subinducent sectas perditionis, et etiam Dominum qui eos redemit abnegantes, accersentes sibi celerem interitum.
2. And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of.
2. Et multi sequentur eorum exitia, per quos via veritatis blasphemabitur;
3. And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.
3. Et in avaritia fictis sermonibus de vobis negotiabuntur; quorum judicium pridem non cessat, et quorum perditio non dormitat.

                     </ns0:gap>, is no where (as some observe) in the New-Testament found to signifie <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi>; for in <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.4. (which some al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge) it is best rendred <ns0:hi>by; Glory</ns0:hi> being there put for God's power, and therefore our Margin here reads it <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> Glory and Virtue; which may either be, by an <ns0:hi>Hendiadis,</ns0:hi> for gorious Virtue, taking Virtue for Power, that glorious Power of God, which is put forth in calling us, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 1.18, 19. or his Goodness and Mercy which appears in the same Calling, in which sense the word may be understood, See <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 3.4, 5. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.9. or (which comes to the same) Glory being often taken for Power, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2.11. by <ns0:hi>Glory</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Virtue</ns0:hi> may be meant God's Power, and Goodness, or Mercy.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:587" />4 Whereby <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This word may be rendred, <ns0:hi>is that, for that, in as much as,</ns0:hi> and then this is an Explication of the things that per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain to Life and Godliness, to Glory and Virtue, all those things being contained in the Promises; or <ns0:hi>whereby</ns0:hi> may be understood of the Glory and Virtue last mentioned, taking them in the latter sense explained, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> by which glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious Goodness and Mercy to us.</ns0:note> are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By Promises we may understand either the matter of the Promises, the things promised, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.36. such as Redemption by Christ, Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />conciliation, Adoption, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and then they are called exceed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing great and precious, in comparison of all temporal and worldly things; or else the Promises themselves, which are called <ns0:hi>great,</ns0:hi> because of the Excellency of the things contain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in them, and <ns0:hi>precious</ns0:hi> in Relation to us; great Things being not only contained in the Promises, but by them secured to us.</ns0:note>, that by these ye might be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 12.10. 1 Joh. 3.2.</ns0:note> partakers of the divine nature <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">We are said to be Partakers of the Divine Nature, not by any Communication of the Divine Essence to us, but by God's impressing upon us, and infusing into us those divine Qualities and Dispositions (Knowledge, Righteousness, and true Holiness) which do express and resemble the Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections of God, and are called his Image, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.24. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.10. And we are said to be made Partakers of this Divine Nature by the Promises of the Gospel, because they are the effectual means of our Regeneration (in which that Divine Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture is communicated to us) by reason of that quickning Spirit which accompanieth them, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.6. works by them, and forms in us the Image of that Wisdom; Righteousness, and Holiness of God, which appears in them; or of that <ns0:hi>Glory of the Lord,</ns0:hi> which, when by Faith we behold in the Glass of Gospel-Promises, we are <ns0:hi>changed into the same Image, even as by the Spirit of the Lord,</ns0:hi> 2 Cor. 3.18. Or, the Divine Nature may be understood of the Glory, and Immortality of the other Life, wherein we shall be conformed to God, and whereof by the Promises we are made Partakers.</ns0:note>, having escaped the corruption <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther by Corruption here we are to understand, 1. <ns0:hi>Destruction,</ns0:hi> to which the greatest Part of the World is obnoxious through Lust, and then Corruption must be opposed to <ns0:hi>Life,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> before, and <ns0:hi>Lust</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Virtue</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Godliness</ns0:hi>: Or, 2. rather all the <ns0:hi>Pravity</ns0:hi> or Wickedness of human Nature, which is here said to be, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to reign and prevail in the World, or worldly Men through Lust, or habitual Concupiscence, which is the Spring and Root from which it proceeds, and then the sense is the same as <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.24. This <ns0:hi>Corruption</ns0:hi> through Lust is opposed to the <ns0:hi>Divine Nature</ns0:hi> before, and <ns0:hi>escaping</ns0:hi> this Corruption agrees with being <ns0:hi>Partakers</ns0:hi> of that Divine Nature. See <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.22, 23, 24. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.9, 10.</ns0:note> that is in the world through lust.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And besides this <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Here the Apostle begins his Exhortation, that since God had done so much for them, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3, 4. they would likewise do their Duty; and that their care and diligence in improving the Grace they had received, might be added to his Bounty in giving it them.</ns0:note>, giving all diligence, and <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>minister unto</ns0:hi>; or it may be a Meta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phor taken from the ancient way of Dancing, in which they joyned Hands one with another, thereby helping, and holding up one another. <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> is here set forth as the first Grace, and which (as it were) leads up, the rest following it, and attending upon it, yet all in conjunction one with another.</ns0:note> to your faith <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Faith is set in the first place as the prime Grace of a Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian, the Foundation and Root of all other, as being that without which nothing else can be pleasing to God, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.6.</ns0:note>, vertue <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Virtue</ns0:hi> he seems to understand Universal Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, or a Complication of all those Graces by which Faith is wont to work; and this being more general, he proceeds from it to o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ers that are more special.</ns0:note>; and to vertue, knowledge <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">By this may be meant spiritual Prudence, which governs and directs other Vertues in their actings; and it is called <ns0:hi>Knowledge,</ns0:hi> because it consists in the practical Knowledge of the Will of God. See 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.6. and 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.7.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And to knowledg, temperance <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">A Grace which represseth, and curbs in, not only sensual Lusts, but all inordinate Appetites, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.22. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.8.</ns0:note>; and to temperance, patience <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">That Christian Fortitude whereby we bear Afflictions and Injuries, so as to persevere in our Duty without being moved by the Evils that attend us in the doing of it.</ns0:note>; and to patience, godli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spects our immediate Duty to God, and comprehends all the Duties of the first Table<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> This is joyned to Patience, as being that which teacheth us, in all we suffer, to acknowledge God's Providence, and Promises of Deliverance, and Recom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pence.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And to godliness, brotherly kindness <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A love to those that are of the Houshold of Faith. This is joyned to Godliness, to shew that it is in vain to pretend to true Religion, and yet be destitute of brotherly Love.</ns0:note>; and to brotherly kindness, charity <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This is more general than the former, and relates to all Men, even our Enemies themselves.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 For if these things be in you and abound <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">If ye not only have these Graces in you, but abound, or grow in them, both as to the inward degree, and outward Exercise of them.</ns0:note>, they make <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either they make you, or declare you not to be barren, or both; they will be both the Causes and Evidences of your not being barren.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>you that ye shall</ns0:hi> neither <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>idle</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> bar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ren <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>slothful, idle, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />active.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Tit. 3.14.</ns0:note> nor unfruitful <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Void of good Works, which are frequently com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pared to Fruits, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 3.10. and 7.17, 18, 19. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.22.</ns0:note> in the knowledge <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Faith of Christ. But more is implied here, than expressed, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> they will make you be active and fruitful in the Knowledge of Christ, and declare you to be so, and thereby make it appear, that ye have not in vain learned Christ.</ns0:note> of our Lord Jesus Christ.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 But he that lacketh these things <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">He that doth not live in the Exercise of the fore-men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned Graces.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Joh. 2.9, 11.</ns0:note> is blind <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Spiritually blind, as being destitute of saving Knowledge.</ns0:note>, and cannot see afar off <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word is variously translated; the most probable account of it is either, 1. that it signifies to <ns0:hi>feel</ns0:hi> the way, or <ns0:hi>grope</ns0:hi> as blind Men do; and then the meaning is, He that lacketh these things in blind, and as a blind Man, gropes, not knowing which way to go; he is really destitute of the Knowledge he pretends to: Or, 2ly, to be <ns0:hi>pore-blind,</ns0:hi> or short-sighted, so as to see things near hand, but not <ns0:hi>afar off,</ns0:hi> as our Translation hath it; and then the sense is, That such a one sees only the things of the World, but cannot look so far as Heaven to discern things there, which if he did, he would walk in the way that leads thither, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> in the Practice of the Duties before prescribed.</ns0:note>, and hath for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gotten that he was purged from his old sins <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">He is judged in the sight of God, to forget a Benefit re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived, that is not effectually mindful of it, in living sutably to it. And so here, he that professeth himself to have been purged from his old Sins, in Justification and Santification, by the Blood and Spirit of Christ, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.11. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 5.25, 26, 27. and yet still lives in Sin, and in the neglect of the Duty he is engaged to, practically declares his Forgetful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of the Mercy he professeth to have been vouchasafed him; and accordingly may be interpreted, to have forgotten it, in that he acts like one that had. Or, if this be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood of one that is really purged from his old Sins, yet he may be said to forget that so far as he returns again to them, or lives not up to the ends of his Purgation, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 1.74, 75.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:588" />10 Wherefore the rather, brethren, give dili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gence <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> In the Exercise of the forementioned Graces.</ns0:note> to <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Joh. 3.19.</ns0:note> make your calling <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Your effectual Calling to the Faith of Christ.</ns0:note>, and election <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Your e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternal Election to Grace and Glory.</ns0:note> sure <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not in respect of God; whose Counsel is in it self sure and stable, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.29. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.19. but in respect of your selves, who may best discern the cause by its effects, and so your Election by your good Works to which you were chosen, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 1.4. and which prove your Calling, (as being the proper genuine Fruits of it, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.1, 2. &c.) as that doth Election from whence it proceeds, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 13.48. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.30.</ns0:note>: for if ye do these things <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The things prescribed, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5, 6, 7.</ns0:note>, ye shall never fall <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not wholly apostatize from God's ways, nor so fall through Temptation into any Sin, as not to recover out of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 For so an entrance shall be ministred to you abundantly <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>richly</ns0:hi>; while ye <ns0:hi>minister,</ns0:hi> or add one Grace to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, one good Work to another, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. &c. God likewise will <ns0:hi>minister</ns0:hi> (the same word is here used, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5.) or add largely, or richly the Supplies of the Spirit, in Grace, and Strength, and Consolation, and whatsoever is needful for you in the way, whereby your Faith may be increased, your Joy promoted, and your Perseverance secured, till ye come into the Possession of the everlasting Kingdom.</ns0:note> into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Wherefore I will not be negligent <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I will be diligent and careful.</ns0:note> to put you always in remembrance of these things, though you know them <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He prevents an Objection, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> though ye know these things already, yet being things of great moment, and you being beset with Temptations, encompassed about with Infirmities, and while you are on the Earth, being in a Land of Forgetfulness, it is necessary to put you in mind of what you know, that ye may remember to do it. See the like, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.14, 15. and 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.21.</ns0:note>, and be established in the present truth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Truth of the Gospel now revealed to you; that which was the great Subject of the Apostles Preaching and Writings, that Jesus Christ was the Christ; That Redemption was wrought by him; That he was risen from the dead; That whosoever believed on him, should re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive Remission of Sins, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> the Promise made to the Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers being now fulfilled, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 13.32, 33. and what was fu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture under the Old-Testament, being present under the New.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Yea, I think it meet as long as I am in this tabernacle <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">In the Body; <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> having not long to live, I would live to the best purpose, and so as I may do the most Good. He calls his Body a Tabernacle both in respect of its short continuance, its mean Structure, and his laborious life in it.</ns0:note>, to <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 3.1.</ns0:note> stir you up <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To awaken and rouze you up, as ye have need, the Flesh being slothful; and lest ye should by security and slightness lose the Benefit of what ye have learned: where Knowledg is not wanting, yet Admonitions may be useful.</ns0:note>, by putting <ns0:hi>you</ns0:hi> in remembrance.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Deut. 4.21, 22. 2 Tim. 4.6.</ns0:note> Knowing that shortly I must put off <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A Metaphor taken from Garments; the Soul while in the Body, is clothed with Flesh, and Death to the godly is but the putting off their Clothes, and going to Bed, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 57.2.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> my tabernacle <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">See 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.1.</ns0:note>, even as <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Joh. 21.18, 19.</ns0:note> our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 21. Christ tells <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> of the kind of his Death, that it should be violent, but speaks nothing there of the circumstance of the time; and therefore either this Apostle had a twofold Revelation of his Death, the former as to the manner of it, and this latter concerning the time: Or, if this here were no other Revelation but that, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 21. it may be said, that <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18.22. Christ intimates that <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi>'s Death should be before <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi>'s, who should live till he came, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> in Judgment against <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> to destroy it, which <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> now (observing the Affairs of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and considering his Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters words, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 24.) perceived to be nigh at hand; and thence infers, that his own Death was not far off.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Moreover, I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease, to have these things <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Doctrine before delivered concerning Faith in Christ, the Practice of good Works, and their continuance in both.</ns0:note> al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ways <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This may be joyned either to <ns0:hi>endeavour,</ns0:hi> and so relate to the Apostle himself; he would always be diligent, and do his part, that they might have these things in remembrance: or rather, (according to our Translation) to <ns0:hi>having in re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />membrance, Peter</ns0:hi> being now near his end; and therefore this <ns0:hi>always,</ns0:hi> may better refer to them that were to live after him, than to himself that was so soon to die.</ns0:note> in remembrance <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />memorate</ns0:hi> them, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to the Benefit, and Edification of the Church; and this includes their having them in remembrance, but implies something more.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 For we have not followed <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 1.17. & 2.1.</ns0:note> cunningly de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vised fables <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Human Figments artificially contrived, either to please and gratifie Mens Fancies, or to deceive and pervert their Judgment; <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> the things we have preached unto you (the Sum of which is the Power and Coming of our Lord Jesus Christ) are <ns0:hi>the true Sayings of God,</ns0:hi> not the Fictions of Men; and so he may have respect both to Heathenish and Jewish Fables. See 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.4. & 4.7. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.4. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.14.</ns0:note>, when we made known unto you the power <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This relates to the Divine Nature of Christ with its glorious Effects, the efficacy of his Doctrine, the Miracles whereby he con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmed it, and especially his Resurrection from the Dead, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.4.</ns0:note>, and coming <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This respects his Human Nature, his coming in the Flesh, in which he manifested the Power before-men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned; both together contain the Sum of the whole Gospel, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That Christ, the promised <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> is come in the Flesh, and that he was furnished with Power sufficient, and Abili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty to save Sinners to the utmost. Or, Christ's coming here may be his second coming, to which the word here used is for the most part applied in the New-Testament, and where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of his Transfiguration in the following Verse was a Represen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation, and a Fore-runner; and in the Belief of which the Apostle would confirm these Saints against those that scoffed at it, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3, 4.</ns0:note> of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Mat. 17.1, 2, 1 Joh. 1.1. and 4.14.</ns0:note> eye-witnesses of his ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jesty <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">By Christ's Majesty may be understood all that Glory which did shine out in him during the whole time of his abode upon earth, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.14. but especially that more eminent Manifestation of it in his Transfiguration in the next Verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 For he received from God the Father ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nour, and glory <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either Honour and Glory for glorious Honour; or <ns0:hi>Glory</ns0:hi> may relate to that Lustre which appeared in the Body of Christ at his Transfiguration, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 17.2. and <ns0:hi>Honour</ns0:hi> to the Voice which came to him from his Father, and the ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nourable Testimony thereby given him.</ns0:note>, when there came such a voice to him from the excellent glory <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either from Heaven, or from the glorious God the Father of Christ, who, by this Voice, did in a special manner manifest his glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious Presence.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 17.5.</ns0:note> This is <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>I. e.</ns0:hi> This is the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> to often promised, and therefore all that was spoken of the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> in the Law and the Prophets, centers in him.</ns0:note> my beloved Son, in whom <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">This implies not only that Christ is peculiarly the Beloved of the Father, but that all they that are adopted to God by Faith in Christ, are be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loved, and graciously accepted in and through him, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 3.17. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 17.26. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 1.6.</ns0:note> I am well-plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 And this voice which came from heaven we <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">I, and <ns0:hi>Iames,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn.</ns0:hi> The Apostle avoucheth him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self to have been an Ear-witness, as well as; Eye-witness of Christ's Glory, hereby intimating that there was as much certainty of the Gospel, even in an <ns0:hi>human</ns0:hi> way, as could possibly be obtained of any thing that is done in the World, seeing Men can be <ns0:hi>humanly</ns0:hi> certain of nothing more, than of what they perceive by their Senses: compare 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.1, 3.</ns0:note> heard <ns0:hi>r,</ns0:hi> when we were with him in the holy <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">So called, not because of any inherent Holiness in it, but because of the extraordinary Manifestation of God's Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence there, in the same sense as the <ns0:hi>Ground</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>holy</ns0:hi> where God appeared to <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ioshua,</ns0:hi> Exod. 3.5. <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 5.15.</ns0:note> mount.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 We have also a more sure word of pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phecy <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> having proved the certainty of the Evangelical Doctrine, by their Testimony that had seen Christ's Glory in his Transfiguration, and heard the Father's Testimony of him, now proves the same by the Testimony of the Prophets under the Old-Testament, and calls the word of Prophecy <ns0:hi>a more sure Word,</ns0:hi> comparing it either, 1. with the Voice from Heaven, then which he calls the word of Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phecy more firm or sure, not in respect of Truth (which was equal in both) but in respect of the manner of its Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />velation, the Voice from Heaven being transient, and heard only by three Apostles; whereas the Word of Prophecy was not only received by the Prophets from God, but by his Command committed to Writing, confirmed by a Succes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of their fellow-Prophets in their several Generations, and approved by Christ himself, and by him preferred before Miracles themselves, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 16.29, 31. Or, 2. with the Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stimony of <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> and the other two Apostles concerning that Voice which came to Christ, than which Testimony the Word of Prophecy is said to be more sure; not<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> simply and it in self, but in respect of those to whom the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle writ; it was more firm in their Minds who had recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved it; or, more sure as to them that were <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and had so fully entertained the writings of the Prophets, and had them in so great Veneration, being confirmed by the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent of so many Ages; whereas the Testimony of these Apostles did not so fully appear to them to be Divine, as not being heretofore expressed in Scripture.</ns0:note>, whereunto ye do well that ye take heed <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That ye search and study it, subject your Consciences to the Power of it, and order your Conversations according to it.</ns0:note>, as unto <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 5.35.</ns0:note> a light <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Lamp,</ns0:hi> to which the Word is often compared, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119.105. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 6.23. Because, as a Lamp, or Candle lighted, dispells the Darkness, and gives Light to those that are in the House, or Room where it is; so the Word gives Light to all that are in God's House, as the Church is called, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.15.</ns0:note> that shineth in a dark place <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>Dirty,</ns0:hi> squalid, because places that have no Light, are usually filthy; the Dirt which is not seen is not remo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved.</ns0:note>, until the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rev. 2.28. & 22.16.</ns0:note> day dawn, and the day-star <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either, 1. The last day called <ns0:hi>the Day</ns0:hi> by way of excellency, because when it once begins, it will never end, and will be all Light without any Darkness; and then what is said of the Word of Prophecy, is to be understood of the whole Scripture; and the sense is, that whereas the whole time of this Life is but a kind of Night of Error and Igno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance, God hath set up his Candle, given us the Light of the Scripture to guide us, and lead us till we come to the glorious Light of the future Life, in which we shall have no need of the Light of the Scripture to direct us, but shall see God as he is, and Face to Face, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.12. According to this Exposition, the <ns0:hi>dawning of the Day,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Day-Star ari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing,</ns0:hi> do not signify different parts of the same day, but rather the whole Day as opposed to that Darkness which would totally over-spread us, were it not for the Light the Word affords us: Our Minds of themselves are dark, in them the Light of the Word shines, and dispells the Darkness by de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grees, according as the Spirit gives us more understanding of it, but yet the Darkness will not be wholly removed, till the Day of Eternal Life dawn upon us, and the Day-Star of the perfect Knowledg of God in the Beatifical Visi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on arise in our hearts. Or, 2. By the Day-dawning, and the Day-Star arising, may be understood a more full, clear, and explicit Knowledg of Christ, and the Mysteries of the Gospel; and then this relates particularly to the Prophecies of the Old-Testament; and, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> calls the times of the Old-Testament, a <ns0:hi>Night, Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.12. as being a time of Darkness and Shadows, in comparison of the Light, and Knowledg of Christ under the New-Testament; so <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> here compares the Writings of the Prophets to a Candle, which gives some, but less Light, and the Preaching of the Gospel to the Day-dawning, and Day-star arising; and commends these Christian <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> to whom he writ, for making use of, and attending to, even this lesser Light, till they attained to greater degrees of Illumination, and the Day-Star of a more full and clear knowledg of Christ, as revealed in the Gospel, did arise in their Hearts. This Exposition is fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />voured by <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 17.11. they there, and so the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verts here, did search the Scriptures, to see if the things spoken by the Apostles did agree with what was before written by the Prophets; and as they there, so these here, are commended for their diligence in so doing, and inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mation given them, that they must attend to the Light of the Old-Testament-Prophecies, till they were thereby led into a greater knowledg and understanding of the Gospel-revelation.</ns0:note> arise in your hearts.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:588" />20 Knowing this first <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either, principally and above other things, as being most worthy to be known; or, knowing this as the first Prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciple of Faith, or the first thing to be Believed.</ns0:note> that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 12.6.</ns0:note> no prophecy of the Scripture is of any private interpreta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word here used, may be rendred, either, 1. as our Translators do <ns0:hi>Interpretation</ns0:hi> or Explication, and then the meaning is, not that private Men are not to interpret the Scripture, only refer all to the Church<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but that no Man, nor Company of Men, no Church nor publick Officers are to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpret the Scripture of their own Heads, according to their own Minds, so as to make their private sence be the sence of the Scripture, but to seek the understanding of it from God, who shews them the meaning of the Word in the Word it self (the more obscure places being expounded by the more clear) and by his Spirit leads Believers in their searching the Scripture, into the understanding of his Mind in it. God himself being the Author of the Word, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21. is the best Interpreter of it: Or, 2 <ns0:hi>Mission</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Dimission,</ns0:hi> a Metaphor taken from Races, where they that ran, were let loose from the Stage where the Race began, that they might run their Course. The Prophets in the Old-Testament are said to <ns0:hi>Run,</ns0:hi> as being God's Messengers, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 23.21. and God is said to <ns0:hi>send</ns0:hi> them, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 13.6, 7. and then this doth not immediately concern the Interpretation of the Scripture, but the first Revelation of it, spoken of in the next Verse; and the question is not, Who hath Authority to Interpret the Scripture now written? but, What Authority the Pen-Men had to write it? and consequently, what respect is due to it? and, why Believers are so carefully to take heed to it. And then the meaning is, that it is the first Principle of our Faith, that the Scripture is not of Human Invention, but Divine Inspiration; that the Prophets writ not their own private Sence in it, but the Mind of God; and at his Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand, not their own Pleasure.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Tim. 3.16. 1 Pet. 1.11.</ns0:note> the prophecy <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Prophetical Writings, or Word of Prophecy, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note> came not <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>at any time.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in old time by the will of man <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Prophets spake not of themselves what and when they pleased,</ns0:note>, but holy men of God <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Prophets, called Men of God, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2.27. and 9.6. and 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 17.18. and elsewhere. They are here called <ns0:hi>Holy,</ns0:hi> not only because of their Lives wherein they were examples to others, but because they were the spe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cial instruments of the Holy Ghost, who sanctified them to the work of Preaching, and Penning what he Dictated to them.</ns0:note>, spake <ns0:hi>as they were</ns0:hi> moved <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>carried out,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>acted, i. e.</ns0:hi> elevated above their own natural abilities. This may imply the illumination of their Minds with the knowledg of Divine Mysteries, the gift of Infallibility, that they might not err, of Prophecy to fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tell things to come, and a peculiar instinct of the Holy Ghost, whereby they were moved to Preach or Write.</ns0:note> by the Holy Ghost.</ns0:p>
